rationale: Start with a broad mid-temperature scouting gradient to elute all 10 compounds if possible and map the overall elution window. This should reveal whether peaks are compressed early or late and give a baseline for later slope and temperature refinement.

All compounds eluted well within the gradient, so trim the solvent window to just cover the observed elution range and keep the separation power focused where the peaks are. This should reduce gradient steepness substantially and test whether the close cluster around peaks 5–7 can be spread further without risking truncation.

The narrowed window improved resolution but cost too much time, so now test pure slope response in the original broad window by making the gradient steeper. Comparing this directly with injection 1 will show whether the critical mid-cluster is strongly slope-sensitive and may improve CRF by shortening the run while keeping all peaks resolved.

The 10 min gradient is faster but over-compresses the critical 5–7 cluster, while 20 min resolves it well but costs CRF on time. An intermediate slope should recover enough resolution for that pair while likely keeping the run short enough to preserve or improve the score.

The key tradeoff is now localized to the 6/7 pair, and moving from 10 to 14 min improved it strongly; a slightly shallower gradient should push that pair closer to full baseline separation while likely staying in the zero time-penalty region. This refines around the current optimum without changing the selectivity framework.

At fixed solvent program, the remaining limitation is selectivity of the 6/7 pair, which may respond more to temperature than to further slope changes. A 5 °C drop should modestly alter relative retention while keeping the run near the current optimum time.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity by collapsing a different pair, so test the opposite direction to see whether modestly higher temperature improves the critical mid-cluster. This keeps the successful 14 min slope while probing whether temperature can lift the resolution term above the current best.

Temperature shifts both hurt selectivity, so stay at 40 C and instead slightly narrow the upper end of the gradient to reduce effective steepness around the elution zone without adding run time. Since the last peak still elutes well before the gradient end, lowering phi1 a notch should keep all peaks in-gradient while potentially opening the 6/7 pair.

Reducing phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the critical 6/7 resolution while preserving zero time penalty, so continue one more step in the same direction. The last peak is still comfortably inside the gradient, making this a strong candidate to further lift the resolution term toward 1.000.

At phi1 = 0.85 the resolution term reached 1.000 but incurred a small time penalty, so try a slightly steeper gradient at the better-shaped phi1 = 0.90 setting to recover time while keeping the 6/7 pair near the threshold. This directly tests whether the current best can be improved by shaving run time without losing too much selectivity.

The 0.90/14 min method is currently best, and the 0.85/14 min run suggests a little more spreading can fully resolve the critical pair at only slight time cost. Increasing tG to 16 min at phi1 0.90 tests whether that pair crosses into full resolution while preserving a near-zero time penalty.

Slope and upper-end window are close to optimal, but the last unresolved gain may come from selectivity rather than more spreading. A larger temperature shift downward than 35 C tests whether the 6/7 pair can separate differently enough at the current best solvent program to outperform the 40 C optimum.

Large downward temperature shifts strongly disrupt selectivity, so test a larger upward shift instead at the current best solvent program. This is the remaining clean way to check for a temperature-selectivity sweet spot before focusing purely on fine solvent-window optimization around the best method.

The best region is clearly near phi1 = 0.85–0.90 at 40 C, with 0.85 giving full resolution but a small time penalty and 0.90 giving the best CRF. A 12 min gradient at phi1 = 0.85 tests whether we can retain the full-resolution behavior of the narrower window while pulling the runtime back into the zero-penalty regime.

Most evidence favors 0.90/14/40 as the optimum, but one remaining unexplored edge case is the lowest allowed temperature at that solvent program. This checks whether a stronger selectivity shift than 30 C might separate the critical cluster differently enough to beat the current best, despite the earlier deterioration at 30–35 C.

Temperature exploration is exhausted and the best region is clearly around 40 C with a narrowed upper solvent limit. Since lowering phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 and then 0.85 improved the critical pair before time penalty appeared, test 0.80 at the same 14 min to see whether full resolution can be achieved with only a minimal additional time cost.

The upper-end narrowing helped, but phi0 has only been tested at 0.05 in the good region and the first peak still elutes with substantial retention. Raising phi0 one step may slightly reshape the solvent window around the crowded middle cluster and reduce unnecessary early gradient space, potentially improving selectivity without extending run time.

Raising phi0 to 0.10 improved the best method, and lowering phi1 previously increased the critical 6/7 resolution but at some time cost. Combining both favorable changes may push the resolution term to 1.000 while still keeping the run close enough to the zero-penalty region to challenge the current best.

We have already reached the maximum CRF, so this run is only to confirm the local optimum boundary without repeating the best method. Lowering phi1 one more step tests whether the method remains on the plateau or begins to incur time penalty, strengthening confidence that 0.10/0.85/14/40 is the robust optimum.

With the optimum already found, the most informative remaining boundary check is whether phi0 can be raised further while preserving the perfect score. This tests if compressing the early window slightly more can keep all peaks resolved and still avoid any time penalty, or if 0.10 is truly the best lower bound.

We now know the optimum lies on a broad plateau, so continue pushing phi0 upward to find its edge. The first peak is getting close to the dead-time region, and this run tests whether further compression of the low-organic end still preserves full performance or starts to under-retain the earliest component.

Phi0 = 0.15 also gives the maximum score, so test whether pairing that stronger lower bound with the slightly wider upper limit retains the CRF plateau. This maps the top ridge more completely and checks whether the perfect region extends diagonally in phi-space.

The remaining unexplored corner around the perfect plateau is the combination of phi0 = 0.15 with a tighter upper bound. This will show whether the ridge of maximal CRF extends toward lower phi1 or whether 0.85 is the lower useful limit before time penalty appears.

Two methods already achieve the maximum CRF, so use the remaining injections to define the plateau boundary in gradient time at the best solvent window. Shortening tG tests whether the perfect-scoring region extends to a faster method or whether 14 min is the minimum needed to keep all pairs fully resolved.

For the final run, test whether the other perfect-scoring solvent window can tolerate a shorter gradient. This brackets the time boundary of the plateau around both maxima and checks whether 0.15/0.85 might sustain full CRF at lower tG better than 0.10/0.85 did.
